title: What is Django and MVT architecture
content:
**Django is a high-level Python web framework** that helps you build secure, maintainable websites quickly. It handles much of the hassle of web development, like URL routing, database interaction, and templating, so you can focus on building your app’s features.

**MVT Architecture:**
Django follows the Model-View-Template (MVT) pattern:

✅ **Model**: Handles the data and database layer (e.g., defining tables, fields, relationships).
✅ **View**: Contains the logic that processes requests and returns responses (e.g., fetching data from models and passing it to templates).
✅ **Template**: The HTML part responsible for rendering the data into a user-friendly format.

**In short:**

Model -> data & business logic

View -> takes request, processes data, returns response

Template -> presentation layer (HTML)

title: What is MVT architecture
content:
✅ **Model**
• This handles the data: it defines the structure of your database tables (fields, relations).

• You write Python classes that inherit from django.db.models.Model.

• Django uses its **ORM (Object Relational Mapper)** to convert these classes into SQL and manage the database automatically.
[code-snippet-0]


✅ **View**
• Views process requests and return responses.

• They fetch data from the Model and pass it to the Template.

• In Django, views are usually Python functions or classes that handle request/response logic.

[code-snippet-1]

✅ **Template**
• Templates are responsible for presentation: rendering HTML pages dynamically using data passed from the View.

• Django uses its own templating language to insert variables, loops, and conditionals into HTML safely.


[code-snippet-2]


**✅ How the Flow Works**
1. User sends request → URL dispatcher maps it to View

2. View interacts with Model to get data → passes data to Template

3. Template generates final HTML → sends response back to user

title: Types of ViewSet and when we use what?
content:
In Django REST Framework (DRF), **ViewSets **are used to simplify the creation of views for **RESTful APIs**. Instead of writing individual methods for** handling HTTP verbs like GET, POST, etc., you define a ViewSet and DRF handles routing automatically** (especially when using routers).


[code-snippet-0]


**1. ViewSet **
^• Use When: You want full control over each action (list, create, retrieve, etc.)

^• You Write: All logic yourself.

^• Example Use Case: Custom business logic for each HTTP method.
[code-snippet-1]


**2. GenericViewSet **
^• Use When: You want flexibility with built-in mixins (ListModelMixin, CreateModelMixin, etc.)

^• You Compose: Only the functionality you need.

^• Example Use Case: Only list and create support, no update/delete.
[code-snippet-2]


**3. ReadOnlyModelViewSet**
^• Use When: API is read-only (e.g., public product catalog, FAQs)

^• Provides: list() and retrieve() methods

^• No Create/Update/Delete
[code-snippet-3]


**4. ModelViewSet**
^• Use When: You need full CRUD operations

^• Provides: All actions (list, retrieve, create, update, partial_update, destroy)

^• Quick and Powerful

[code-snippet-4]


**Summary Decision Guide**
[code-snippet-5]
codeSnippets:
| Type                   | Base Class                                     | Purpose                                                              |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ViewSet`              | `rest_framework.viewsets.ViewSet`              | Manual control over all methods (`list`, `retrieve`, `create`, etc.) |
| `GenericViewSet`       | `rest_framework.viewsets.GenericViewSet`       | Combine with mixins for flexibility                                  |
| `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` | `rest_framework.viewsets.ReadOnlyModelViewSet` | Only allows `GET` (`list` and `retrieve`)                            |
| `ModelViewSet`         | `rest_framework.viewsets.ModelViewSet`         | Full CRUD support out of the box                                     |
class CustomViewSet(ViewSet):
    def list(self, request):
        ^# Custom list logic
        pass

    def create(self, request):
        ^# Custom create logic
        pass
from rest_framework.mixins import ListModelMixin, CreateModelMixin

class ListCreateViewSet(ListModelMixin, CreateModelMixin, GenericViewSet):
    queryset = Post.objects.all()
    serializer_class = PostSerializer
class PostReadOnlyViewSet(ReadOnlyModelViewSet):
    queryset = Post.objects.all()
    serializer_class = PostSerializer
class PostViewSet(ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Post.objects.all()
    serializer_class = PostSerializer
| Scenario                 | Recommended ViewSet          |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| Custom logic needed      | `ViewSet`                    |
| Only some methods needed | `GenericViewSet` with mixins |
| Read-only API            | `ReadOnlyModelViewSet`       |
| Full CRUD API            | `ModelViewSet`               |

title: What is a Django project vs app?
content:
In Django, the **terms Project and App have specific meanings**, and understanding the difference is crucial when organizing your code.

**🏗️ Django Project  (django-admin startproject projectname) **
A project is the entire web application or website you're building.
It contains configuration settings and can contain multiple apps.

🔹 Characteristics:
  **• Created using  django-admin startproject projectname**

• Manages the overall settings, URLs, and dependencies

• Contains files like:

**📦 Django App   (python manage.py startapp appname)**
An app is a modular component of your project that does one thing — like handling blog posts, users, comments, payments, etc.

🔹 Characteristics:
• Created using python manage.py startapp appname

• Can be reused across multiple projects

title: How does Django handle HTTP requests?
content:
**🔁 Django Request-Response Lifecycle**
**1. HTTP Request from Browser**
• A user visits a URL in their browser (e.g., https://example.com/blog/5), which sends an HTTP request to the server hosting the Django app.

**2. Web Server Gateway (WSGI/ASGI)**
• Django uses WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface) or ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) to communicate with web servers like Gunicorn, uWSGI, or Daphne.

• The WSGI/ASGI server passes the request to the Django application.

• 🔧 File involved: wsgi.py or asgi.py


**3. Django Creates a HttpRequest Object**
• Django converts the raw request into a HttpRequest object, which contains metadata such as:

• GET, POST data

• Headers

• Cookies

• Path and method (GET, POST, etc.)

• User info (if authenticated)
[code-snippet-0]

**4. Middleware Processing**
• Django passes the request through a middleware stack defined in settings.py under MIDDLEWARE.

**Middleware functions can:**
• Process requests before the view runs

• Modify responses after the view runs

• Handle exceptions, authentication, security, etc.

[code-snippet-1]

**Example: Checking if the user is authenticated, adding CORS headers, etc.**

**5. URL Routing (urls.py)**
Django matches the request URL against patterns defined in your urls.py files.

[code-snippet-2]
If it matches blog/5/, Django routes it to the corresponding view: views.blog_detail(request, id=5)

**6. View Function Executes**
The view handles the logic based on the request.

It may interact with:

• Models (to query the database)

• Forms (to validate user input)

• Templates (to render HTML)


[code-snippet-3]

**7. Template Rendering (if applicable)**
• If the view uses render(), it loads the HTML template, fills in dynamic data (context), and returns a fully-rendered HTML response.

[code-snippet-4]

**8. Response Object (HttpResponse)**
The view returns an HttpResponse or JsonResponse, which Django then processes through response middleware.

[code-snippet-5]

**9. Back through Middleware (Response Phase)**
The HttpResponse goes back through the middleware (reverse order), allowing middleware to:

• Modify the response

• Add headers

• Handle caching, compression, etc.

**10. HTTP Response Sent to Browser**
Finally, Django sends the response (HTML, JSON, file, redirect, etc.) back to the user's browser.

[code-snippet-6]
codeSnippets:
from django.http import HttpRequest
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    ...
]
urlpatterns = [
    path('blog/<int:id>/', views.blog_detail),
]
def blog_detail(request, id):
    post = Blog.objects.get(pk=id)
    return render(request, 'blog/detail.html', {'post': post})
render(request, 'template.html', {'data': value})
from django.http import HttpResponse

return HttpResponse("Here is your blog post!")
Browser
  ↓
WSGI/ASGI Server
  ↓
Django Request Object
  ↓
Middleware (request phase)
  ↓
URL Dispatcher (urls.py)
  ↓
View Function (logic + DB)
  ↓
Template Rendering (if needed)
  ↓
Response Object
  ↓
Middleware (response phase)
  ↓
WSGI/ASGI Server
  ↓
Browser (Response shown)

title: 📦 What is a Model in Django?
content:
**A Model in Django is a Python class** that defines the structure of your **database tables. **It acts as a bridge between your Python code and the database using **Django’s Object-Relational Mapper (ORM).**

✅ **Why Use Django Models? **
• Automatically creates SQL tables for you.

• Lets you interact with the database using Python (no raw SQL).

• Ensures consistency between your app and your DB schema.
[code-snippet-0]
codeSnippets:
# myapp/models.py

from django.db import models

class BlogPost(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    content = models.TextField()
    author = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

title: What is ORM in Django?
content:
**ORM stands for Object-Relational Mapper**. In Django, the **ORM allows developers to interact with the relational database (like PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite) using Python code instead of SQL.**


It acts as **a bridge between Python objects and database tables, **so you can create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) data using simple Python syntax.

**🔧 Example (Plain SQL vs Django ORM)**
**SQL**

[code-snippet-0]

**Django ORM**

[code-snippet-1]

**🧱 How It Works:**
• Each model class you define maps to a table in the database.

• Each attribute in the model is a column in the table.

• Django provides a QuerySet API to interact with the database using model methods.

content:
**Django generic views are pre-built class-based views (CBVs) **that help you handle common patterns like displaying a list,** showing a single object, creating, updating, or deleting objects — without writing repetitive boilerplate code.**

**🧱 Common Types of Generic Views:**

🧰 Example: Blog App Using Generic Views

| `ListView`   | Show a list of objects             |

from django.db import models

class BlogPost(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    content = models.TextField()
from django.views.generic import ListView, DetailView
from .models import BlogPost

class BlogListView(ListView):
    model = BlogPost
    template_name = 'blog_list.html'
    context_object_name = 'posts'

class BlogDetailView(DetailView):
    model = BlogPost
    template_name = 'blog_detail.html'
    context_object_name = 'post'
from django.urls import path
from .views import BlogListView, BlogDetailView

urlpatterns = [
    path('', BlogListView.as_view(), name='blog-list'),
    path('<int:pk>/', BlogDetailView.as_view(), name='blog-detail'),
]

title: What is the difference between filter(), get(), and all()?
content:
**🔍 1. all()**
✅ What it does:
• Returns all objects in the queryset (like SELECT * in SQL).
✅ Use Case:
• When you want to list all rows from a table (e.g., show all blog posts).


[code-snippet-0]

**🔎 2. filter()**
**✅ What it does:**
• Returns a QuerySet of objects that match the given conditions.
 If no match, returns an empty QuerySet — doesn’t raise an error.

**✅ Use Case:**
• When you need to search or filter records based on one or more conditions.

• Safe to use when you're unsure if matching data exists.
[code-snippet-1]

**🔐 3. get()**
**✅ What it does:**
• Returns a single object that matches the condition.
If:

• No match → raises DoesNotExist exception

• More than one match → raises MultipleObjectsReturned exception

**✅ Use Case:**
• When you are sure that only one unique object should match (e.g., fetching by primary key or unique field).



[code-snippet-2]

**Summary**

[code-snippet-3]
codeSnippets:
from myapp.models import BlogPost

posts = BlogPost.objects.all()
posts_by_author = BlogPost.objects.filter(author="Shubham")
post = BlogPost.objects.get(id=1)
| Method     | Returns       | Error on No Match?   | Multiple Matches?               | Use When…                              |
| ---------- | ------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `all()`    | All records   | No                   | N/A                             | You want **everything** from a table   |
| `filter()` | QuerySet      | No (returns empty)   | No                              | You want **some or none** (safe query) |
| `get()`    | Single object | Yes (`DoesNotExist`) | Yes (`MultipleObjectsReturned`) | You want **exactly one object**        |

title: ⚙️ How Does Django Handle Middleware?
content:
******Middleware in Django is a framework of hooks into Django’s request/response processing**. It is a layer between the request and view, and between the view and the response.

**Middleware lets you process, modify, or block requests and responses globally — before they reach the view or after they leave it.**

**🔁 Django Request/Response Lifecycle with Middleware**
**🔄 Request Phase: **
• User sends an HTTP request.

• Django processes this request through middleware (top-down).

• If all middleware passes, Django routes the request to the correct view.

**🔄 Response Phase:**
• View returns a response.

• The response passes back through middleware (bottom-up).

• Final response is sent to the browser.

🧱** Structure of Middleware**
Each middleware is a Python class with at least one of these methods:
[code-snippet-0]

**📁 Where Is Middleware Configured?**

In settings.py under the MIDDLEWARE list:

[code-snippet-1]
**Order matters: the request passes through middleware in listed order, and responses return in reverse order**.
**🧰 Use Cases for Middleware:**

[code-snippet-2]
codeSnippets:
class MyMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        # Code before view
        response = self.get_response(request)
        # Code after view
        return response
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',
    ...
    'myapp.middleware.MyCustomMiddleware',  # Your custom one
]
| Purpose                    | Middleware Example           |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Session management         | `SessionMiddleware`          |
| Authentication check       | `AuthenticationMiddleware`   |
| Security headers           | `SecurityMiddleware`         |
| Cross-site request forgery | `CsrfViewMiddleware`         |
| Custom logging             | Your custom middleware class |
| IP banning, rate limiting  | Custom logic in middleware   |
